# Results — Study 88 (Dogs-of-the-Dow) on the real point-in-time tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — each January buy
the **ten highest trailing-12-month-yield** stocks in the **then-current** Dow 30,
equal-weight, hold the calendar year, rebalance, charge **20 bps** on the turnover — run on
**total-return** prices and pinned against the **same-basis** Dow benchmark (DIA total
return). As-of **2026-06-13**; match the fingerprint to confirm you hold the same tape.*

## Sample span & survivorship handling (no silent caps)

- **Universe:** a **point-in-time** Dow-30 membership timeline encoded from public record
  (Wikipedia, *Historical components of the DJIA*), anchored at the **1999-11-01** reshuffle
  — the earliest date this desk can reconstruct the exact 30 with confidence. Each January's
  Dogs are picked **only** from the members as of that January; the timeline replays ~12
  reshuffles forward (GM and Eastman Kodak leave, Apple and Nvidia later enter, etc.).
- **Sample:** **26 January rebalances, 2000 → 2025.** Earlier years are deliberately not
  sampled — a shorter honest window beats a longer survivorship-biased one.
- **Two members left out (named, not silent):** Eastman Kodak (a 2000–2004 member; the old
  entity is bankrupt with no recoverable Yahoo tape) and Walgreens (a 2019–2024 member;
  taken private and delisted late 2024). **29 of 30 names are priced every year**, enough to
  rank and pick a full ten — but both absentees were plausible high-yielders, so this is a
  real, named selection limitation on the Signal axis.

## The honest test — 26 years, net of 20 bps/turnover

| Arm | CAGR | Grew $1 → |
|---|--:|--:|
| **Dogs of the Dow** | **8.51%** | **$8.36** |
| Dow (DIA total return) | 7.54% | $6.61 |

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| CAGR gap (Dogs − Dow) | **+0.98 pts/yr** |
| Mean annual excess | **+0.87%/yr** |
| Win rate (Dogs > Dow) | **54%** (14/26 years) |
| **HAC *t* on the annual excess** | **+0.59**  (\|t\| < 2 → not certifiable) |
| Block-bootstrap 95% CI on mean excess | **[−2.15%, +3.59%]**  (two-sided *p* = 0.51) |
| Alpha (Dogs ~ Dow) | **+2.58%/yr**, *t* = **+1.59** |
| Beta (Dogs ~ Dow) | **0.80**  (R² = 0.72) |

## How to read it

- **There is a modest historical edge — but it does not clear the bar.** Dogs beat the Dow
  by ~1 point/year over 26 years, but the annual excess has **HAC *t* = 0.59** and a
  bootstrap CI that straddles zero (*p* = 0.51). On *this tape* the edge is statistically
  indistinguishable from noise. → Signal **WEAK** (the literature is sympathetic; this
  sample alone can't certify it).
- **Much of what edge there is, is a defensive value tilt — beta you were always paid for.**
  The alpha-vs-beta read gives **beta 0.80** (the Dogs are a *lower*-beta, defensive
  high-yield slice of the Dow) and an alpha of +2.58%/yr that **does not clear *t* = 2**
  (*t* = 1.59). You're buying a cheaper, higher-yield, lower-beta basket — a known risk
  tilt, not a Dow-specific secret.
- **Tradability is FRAGILE, and the friction is taxes, not trading.** Turnover is low
  (~23%/yr), so the gap barely moves from 0 to 100 bps of cost. The binding drag is the
  **tax** on a deliberately high dividend stream a taxable investor pays every year, plus
  the **dividend-trap** risk the trailing-yield screen courts — the January-2009 basket was
  led by Citigroup (22.8% trailing yield) and Bank of America (20.8%), names about to slash
  their payouts. A ~1-point gross gap that isn't statistically real does not survive that.
  → Tradability **FRAGILE**.

## Reproduce

```bash
python examples/verify.py              # real tape (this doc)
python examples/run_synthetic_demo.py  # offline positive/negative control
```
